analysis.one_liner: Gives HMO and insured patients guaranteed emergency coverage, choice of doctors, outside appeals, and the right to sue their insurer.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in March 1998 with 31 Democratic cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and got no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a floor of protections for people in managed care plans and other health coverage. Plans would have to pay for emergency room care without asking permission first, let women see an OB-GYN without a referral, cover routine costs of approved clinical trials, pay for exceptions to drug formularies when a doctor says they're needed, and use outside reviewers that patients can appeal to when care is denied. It would also strip away part of a federal law that currently shields employers and insurers in these plans from being sued for injuries caused by denied care.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 150 million Americans with private health insurance would gain enforceable protections: no pre-authorization for emergency care at in-network prices, direct access to OB-GYNs and standing specialist referrals, coverage of routine costs in NIH-approved clinical trials, medically-necessary exceptions to drug formularies, binding outside appeals for high-stakes denials, minimum 48-hour hospital stays after mastectomy with reconstructive surgery coverage, and the right to sue their insurer or plan administrator in state court for personal injury or wrongful death caused by a coverage decision.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in employer and private health plans

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency services without prior authorization, under a 'prudent layperson' standard, and pay out-of-network emergency providers at in-network rates so patients don't get surprise bills [S2] [S3].

Patients must be offered a choice of coverage with out-of-network providers, can designate an OB-GYN as their primary doctor, and get standing referrals to specialists for ongoing serious conditions [S2] [S3].

Every plan must provide internal appeals with deadlines (72 hours for expedited cases) and a binding external appeals process run by independent, conflict-free entities for denials that endanger health or involve large amounts [S2] [S3].

The bill forbids 'gag clauses' in physician contracts, bans doctor incentive arrangements that reward limiting care, bars retaliation against doctors who report quality problems, and prohibits utilization reviewers from being paid based on the number of claims they deny [S2] [S3].

It amends ERISA so that patients can bring state-law damage suits for personal injury or wrongful death against insurers and plan administrators — the legal change patients' advocates considered the centerpiece, since employer plans were otherwise shielded from lawsuits [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans bear the direct cost: new coverage mandates, network adequacy standards, external appeals they must pay for, and liability exposure under the ERISA carve-out. Employers sponsoring plans face compliance costs and potentially higher premiums, though the bill largely shields employers from lawsuits except when the employer itself decides a claim.

drawbacks.text: Coverage mandates, network adequacy requirements, and binding external appeals raise plan costs, which insurers and employers would likely pass on through higher premiums; critics argued some small employers might respond by dropping coverage or trimming benefits.

Opening employer-related plans to state damage suits (the ERISA amendment) would expose insurers and some plan decision-makers to jury awards, which opponents said would drive up costs and make plan sponsors more defensive in approving care.

The bill adds substantial administrative and reporting duties — quality programs, uniform data collection, disclosure handbooks, state ombudsmen — that mean real overhead costs for every plan and issuer, not just bad actors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address documented harms of 1990s managed care — surprise out-of-network emergency bills, denied referrals, formulary rejections, and reviewers paid to deny claims. The honest cost side is that mandates and litigation exposure would push premiums up, and that cost would spread across all enrollees, while the liability expansion reaches only insurers and administrators, not employers, narrowing who is actually accountable. Most of the package, though, is process and disclosure standards rather than open-ended entitlements, so the cost estimates critics cited were contested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 1998 on March 31, 1998, joined on the original sponsor list by 22 other Democratic senators including Edward Kennedy, Barbara Boxer, and Paul Wellstone [S1] [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day [S1] [S5].
The complete action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, no floor debate, and no vote — the referral was the bill's only action [S5].
The bill applied its protections to group plans, individual coverage, and plans governed by ERISA, and amended ERISA to allow state-law suits for damages from denied care [S2].
The Congress ended January 3, 1999, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, managed care companies, and employer plan sponsors came out ahead: none of the coverage mandates, appeal requirements, or lawsuit exposure in the bill ever became law. Patients in managed care plans were left without federal emergency-coverage, appeal, or liability protections from this bill.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Minority Leader and lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 22 fellow Democrats as original cosponsors

against.name: Jim Jeffords
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill was never reported out of committee

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the chamber instead debated a narrower rival patient-protection bill backed by Republicans in mid-1998

against.name: Managed care industry and business groups
against.role: Health insurers, HMOs, and employer coalitions
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against broad patient-bill-of-rights mandates, especially the ERISA provision exposing insurers to damage suits

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican committee chair and majority leader let the bill sit without action while Senate Republicans advanced their own narrower patient-protection bill.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill imposes coverage mandates, network adequacy rules, binding external appeals, bans on gag clauses and denial-based incentives, and opens insurers to state damage suits under the ERISA carve-out. Its business model of restricting access and paying reviewers to control costs would be regulated from several directions at once.

Plans governed by ERISA must comply with all the new standards, raising compliance and premium costs, but the bill deliberately shields employers from the new lawsuits except when the employer itself decides a claim. Opposed the mandates as a cost burden on workers' benefits.
Plans must pay out-of-network emergency providers at in-network rates and cannot require prior authorization, ending the practice of shifting emergency costs onto patients.
The bill bans contract gag clauses, forbids plans from retaliating against doctors who advocate for patients, requires standing referrals, and requires physician participation in formulary decisions.
